title: DIY VR: How to build your own headset, and why you probably won't want to
gist: Tim Stevens built a DIY VR headset from roughly $180 of parts using the Relativty project and found tracking drift, a fake IMU and poor comfort, concluding most people should pay for a Quest. The piece also frames VR as a cooled market where enthusiast innovation is now the most interesting activity.

insights.claim: VR momentum has been in decline since its post-2016 Oculus Rift surge, with new headset development slowing and many companies including Apple scaling back or shelving efforts.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Consumer XR is a cooled category; expect fewer big-platform launches.
insights.quote: The rate of development of new headsets has slowed, with many companies (including Apple) scaling back or shelving their efforts.

insights.claim: Microsoft is ending support for Windows Mixed Reality, though third-party drivers like OASIS on Steam keep WMR headsets alive.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Platform sunsets push users to community or alternative ecosystems.
insights.quote: Microsoft was nixing support for WMR

insights.claim: The most interesting development in VR now comes from the enthusiast and DIY front, even as new releases like Steam Frame and Pimax Dream Air still appear.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Innovation is migrating from corporate labs to open-source communities.
insights.quote: many of the most interesting developments in the space these days are on the enthusiast front

insights.claim: A DIY headset costs about $180 in components, roughly half the price of a Meta Quest 3S, but the author's total came to $239.93 after breaking displays.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Cost savings vanish once upgrades and time are included.
insights.quote: My total outlay for this project was $239.93.

insights.claim: Upgrading displays, IMU, battery and housing quickly brings a DIY headset near the cost of a Quest, which works effortlessly out of the box.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Mass-market subsidized hardware is hard to undercut on value.
insights.quote: you’re not far from the cost of that Quest

insights.claim: The author recommends most people pay the extra for a commercial headset because DIY tracking, image quality and comfort are poor.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: DIY VR remains a decidedly niche hobby, not a market threat.
insights.quote: I’d certainly recommend that most people pay the extra.

insights.claim: Core parts are cheap: 2.9-inch 1440x1440 LCDs with controller (~$125), a GY-91 IMU (~$5), and an Arduino Pro Micro (~$5 or less).
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Commodity displays and microcontrollers enable low-cost prototyping of headset hardware.

insights.claim: The author's GY-91 was a cheaper 6500 IMU without the magnetometer, not the 9250 he paid for, a commonplace counterfeit-component problem that substantially degrades tracking.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Component-sourcing fraud is a real cost for hobbyist and low-end hardware supply chains.
insights.quote: this is a disconcertingly commonplace experience

insights.claim: Pressing fragile exposed LCDs into the clips specified by the design broke both displays, adding $62 in cost.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Open-source designs can embed costly flaws that end users discover the hard way.
insights.quote: The exposed LCDs are extremely fragile

insights.claim: Even after recalibration, sensor drift and comfort problems meant the author quit after 15 minutes in iRacing, versus hourslong endurance races in mass-market headsets.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Sensor quality and ergonomics are the key moats for commercial headsets.
insights.quote: After 15 minutes in this one, I was ready to quit.
